place.zh: 沉鼎山 · 后山崖顶 · 青石前
place.en: Mount Chending · The cliff top · before the blue stone

setup.zh: 瞿老捧出一个旧布包：半卷竹简，《河洛剑诀》。三百年，没有一个人练成过第一宫。「你念开篇。」
setup.en: Elder Qu brings out an old cloth bundle: half a bamboo scroll, the He-Luo Sword Canon. In three hundred years no one has mastered its first palace. "Read the opening."

recap.zh: 《河洛剑诀》的开篇，是你娘教你的洛书口诀。瞿老问：「……你娘，是谁？」他倒握扫帚，只动了一下——落叶在半空排成九宫，落成一个缺了中间一笔的「徐」字。
recap.en: The opening of the Heluo Sword Canon was the Luo-diagram rhyme your mother taught you. Elder Qu asked: "…Your mother — who is she?" He turned his broom round and moved once — the leaves hung in nine squares and fell into the character Xu, missing its middle stroke.

zh: 半卷竹简，比《吐纳经》还旧。
en: Half a bamboo scroll, older than the Scroll of Breath.
"Nine on the head, one on the feet, three on the left, seven on the right…"

story.zh:
瞿老道：「剑。」

他转身进了草屋，出来时手里捧着一个布包，布包很旧，边角都磨破了。他把布包放在青石上，一层一层地打开，里面是一卷竹简，比《吐纳经》还旧，只剩下半卷。瞿老道：「这是本观祖师留下的一门剑诀。三百年了，没有一个人练成过一宫。因为它要五行俱全，一行不缺，一行不偏，剑气才转得起来。单灵根练它，走火入魔；三灵根、四灵根练它，一辈子卡在门口。」他看着小满，「五行杂灵根，天底下都笑的那种。我等了五十年。」

小满胸口的木牌烫了一下，那只半透明的小银狐钻了出来，蹲在他肩膀上，看了看瞿老，看了看竹简，又看了看他，眯起眼睛道：「……本王的徒弟，他也配？」

小满吓得一哆嗦，险些一屁股坐在香炉上。瞿老皱了皱眉，往他肩膀上看了一眼，什么都没看见，又看了一眼，道：「你肩膀上，有东西？」小满忙道：「……有、有只虫子。」银月大怒：「你说谁是虫子？！」木牌随即凉了——它走的时候，狠狠地踩了他一脚，隔着衣裳，正踩在他锁骨上。

瞿老又看了他肩膀一眼，没再问，把竹简推到他面前：「《河洛剑诀》。你念开篇。」
story.en:
"Sword," said Elder Qu.

He turned into the grass hut and came out holding a cloth bundle, very old, its corners worn through. He laid it on the bluestone and unwrapped it layer by layer; inside was a bamboo scroll, older than the *Scroll of Breath*, only half of it left. Elder Qu said: "This is a sword canon left by the founder of this temple. In three hundred years no one has mastered even one palace of it. Because it needs all five elements, not one missing, not one lopsided, before the sword qi will turn. A single root that tries it goes mad; three roots, four roots, stick at the door all their lives." He looked at Xiaoman. "A mixed five-element root — the kind the whole world laughs at. I've waited fifty years."

The token on Xiaoman's chest went hot; the half-transparent little silver fox slipped out and sat on his shoulder, looked at Elder Qu, at the bamboo scroll, at him, and narrowed its eyes: "…A disciple of mine — and he thinks he's fit?"

Xiaoman jumped so hard he nearly sat down on the censer. Elder Qu frowned and glanced at his shoulder, saw nothing, glanced again: "Something on your shoulder?" Xiaoman said quickly, "…A b-bug." Yinyue was furious: "Who are you calling a bug?!" and the token went cold — as she left she stamped on him hard, through his clothes, right on the collarbone.

Elder Qu looked at his shoulder once more, asked nothing, and pushed the scroll in front of him: "The *Heluo Sword Canon*. Read the opening."

exits.means: recites the opening of the sword canon

story.zh:
小满低头去看第一行，手却停住了。竹简上的字，有些他认不全；可那几个字的排法——九个，三三一排，中间一个「五」——他实在太熟了。那是灶间的油灯底下，他娘拿九颗刻了记号的栗子，一颗一颗摆给他看的。他不用看竹简，便念了出来：「戴九履一，左三右七，二四为肩，六八为足，五居中央。」

崖顶上很静。一阵风吹过来，香炉里三根香的烟一齐歪了一歪。

瞿老看着他。瞿老扫了五十年地，看过几万个孩子爬那三百级石阶，脸上从来没有过什么表情。这一回，却有了。

他道：「……你没看竹简。」

小满说：「我娘教的。」

瞿老道：「你娘？」

小满说：「她说，是她爹教她的。她爹，是从一本旧书上看来的。」

瞿老沉默了很久很久。久到香炉里的香烧下去了一截，一截香灰无声无息地折断了，落在青石上。他才道：「……你娘，是谁？」

小满张了张嘴，不知道该怎么答。他娘是谁？他娘是石坳村猎户家的媳妇，会织布，会算账，下雨天会把家里所有的盆都摆出来接水，一共十七个；他娘是一个落魄塾师的女儿，识字，嫁了一个不识字的猎户。他娘，还能是谁？

他想了半天，只说出一句：「……我娘，是我外公的闺女。」

瞿老看着他，看了好一会儿，嘴角动了一动，不知是想笑，还是想别的什么。

瞿老没有再问下去。他把竹简卷起来，只露出第一段，卷的时候，手指头在竹简的边上停了一停，像是摸到了一道很旧的刻痕。

瞿老道：「九宫配九州，一宫一州。你听过九州么？」

小满道：「听过。说书先生讲过，天下分九州。」

瞿老道：「谁分的？」

小满道：「……大禹？」

瞿老点点头，道：「大禹治水，治完了水，走遍了天下，把天下分成九块，每一块叫一州，每一州出什么土、种什么田、交什么贡，都记了下来。这一篇东西，叫〈禹贡〉，在《尚书》里头。」他顿了一顿，看着小满，「里头写徐州的那几句，你听好了：『海、岱及淮惟徐州』——东到海，北到泰山，南到淮水，这一块，就是徐州。『淮、沂其乂，蒙、羽其藝』——」

小满一愣：「蒙？」

瞿老道：「蒙山。你家那座山。」

小满张大了嘴。他从小在蒙山底下长大，蒙山上的每一道沟、每一棵栗子树，他闭着眼睛都认得；他从来没想过，他家那座山，四千多年前就已经写在书上了。

瞿老接着道：「徐州往京城里交贡，交的是什么，你猜。」

小满猜不着。

瞿老道：「『厥貢惟土五色』——五种颜色的土。青、红、白、黑、黄，一种一种分开装好，千里迢迢地送去。」他看着小满，「那天在正殿里，测灵石亮了五种颜色，满殿的人笑你。他们笑你是五种碎布拼的一块抹布。」

小满低下头，没说话。

瞿老道：「四千年前，禹王要的，就是这五种颜色的土。」

小满猛地抬起头来。

瞿老没有看他，只看着远处的泗水，又道：「〈禹贡〉里还有一句，『泗濱浮磬』——泗水边上的石头，敲起来像磬一样响。」说着从脚边捡起一块扁扁的青石，拿扫帚把在上头轻轻一敲。

「当——」

那一声不大，却很长，很远，像有人在很远很远的地方敲了一记钟。小满听着那一声，心里忽然一动——他好像在哪里听过这样的一声，可是想不起来是在哪里了。

「巽四在东南，是徐州。」瞿老道，「你是徐州人。今日先教你巽四。泗水，是一切开始的地方。」

他站起身来，把扫帚倒过来握在手里，扫帚头朝下，扫帚把朝前，道：「看好了。」

只动了一下。

小满甚至没看清他是怎么动的，只见崖顶上的落叶——青石上一片也没有，可青石外头的崖边上，积着一冬的落叶——一片不剩，全给卷了起来，在半空里排成一个方方正正的格子，三三一排，共是九格，中间那一格空着。跟着落叶纷纷落下，一片一片，落在崖顶上，落成了一个字：

**徐**

那个字，缺了中间一笔。

瞿老把扫帚靠回墙角，拍了拍手上的灰：「我练了四十年，只练到这一步。中间那一笔，差着一行，填不上。」

小满道：「师父，剑诀叫河洛。洛是洛书，九宫。那河呢？」

瞿老道：「河是河图。」他蹲下来，拿扫帚把在雪地似的落叶上画了一个圈，圈上点了五个点，「河图讲的是五行相生：木生火，火生土，土生金，金生水，水又生木，一样生一样，转成一个圈。剑气要在身子里转，就得这么转——一样生一样，一样也不能缺。缺了一样，圈就断了，断了的地方，剑气便从那里漏出去。」他把其中一个点抹掉，「我缺的是火。四十年，圈上总有一个口子。」

小满看着那个缺了一个点的圈，心里忽然一酸。他想起讲堂上褚先生说他是漏勺，想起秘境石室里银月说，你不是漏勺了，是水缸。原来这天底下，漏的不止他一个。

小满一时说不出话来。

瞿老扛起扫帚往草屋里走，头也不回：「你五行俱全。你把它填上，再来找我。」

走到门口，他又停住了，背对着小满，道：「那颗丹，吃之前，先来问我。」

说罢，进了屋。

小满在崖顶上又站了一会儿，才往山下走。走到半山腰，回头望了一眼。崖顶的草屋门开着，瞿老坐在那张木桌前，一动不动，面前摆着那两只茶杯，一只朝上，一只朝下。隔得远，看不清他在做什么，只看见他坐了很久，一直没有去碰那只朝下的杯子。
story.en:
Xiaoman looked down at the first line, and his hand stopped. Some of the characters he couldn't read; but the way those few were laid out — nine, three to a row, a "five" in the middle — he knew all too well. It was under the oil lamp in the kitchen, his mother setting out nine notched chestnuts one by one for him to see. He didn't need to look at the scroll; he recited it: "Wear nine, tread on one; three on the left, seven on the right; two and four the shoulders, six and eight the feet; five dwells in the centre."

It was very still on the cliff top. A breeze came, and the smoke of the three sticks of incense leaned all together.

Elder Qu looked at him. Elder Qu had swept for fifty years and watched tens of thousands of children climb those three hundred steps, and his face had never shown anything. This time it did.

He said: "…You didn't look at the scroll."

"My mother taught me," said Xiaoman.

"Your mother?"

"She said her father taught her. Her father got it out of an old book."

Elder Qu was silent a long, long while. So long that the incense burned down a section and a column of ash broke off without a sound and fell on the bluestone. Then he said: "…Your mother — who is she?"

Xiaoman opened his mouth and didn't know how to answer. Who was his mother? His mother was a hunter's wife in Stone Hollow, who could weave, could keep accounts, and on rainy days set out every basin in the house to catch the drips, seventeen of them; his mother was a down-at-heel village teacher's daughter who could read and married a hunter who couldn't. Who else could his mother be?

He thought a good while and could only say: "…My mother is my grandfather's girl."

Elder Qu looked at him a long while; the corner of his mouth moved — whether toward a smile or something else, who could say.

Elder Qu asked no more. He rolled up the scroll, leaving only the first passage showing; as he rolled it his finger paused at the edge of the bamboo, as if it had touched a very old notch.

"The nine palaces match the nine provinces," said Elder Qu, "a palace to a province. Have you heard of the nine provinces?"

"I have. The storyteller said the world is divided into nine provinces."

"Who divided it?"

"…Great Yu?"

Elder Qu nodded. "Great Yu tamed the flood, and when it was tamed he walked the whole world and divided it into nine parts, each called a province, and wrote down for each what soil it had, what fields it tilled, what tribute it sent. That piece of writing is called the 'Tribute of Yu,' and it's in the *Book of Documents*." He paused and looked at Xiaoman. "The lines on Xu Province — listen: 'The sea, Mount Dai and the Huai — this is Xu Province.' East to the sea, north to Mount Tai, south to the Huai: that stretch is Xu. 'The Huai and the Yi were brought to order; Meng and Yu were planted —'"

Xiaoman started. "Meng?"

"Meng Mountain. Your mountain."

Xiaoman's mouth fell open. He had grown up at the foot of Meng Mountain and knew every gully and every chestnut tree on it with his eyes shut; it had never occurred to him that his own mountain had been written in a book four thousand years ago.

Elder Qu went on: "And the tribute Xu Province sent to the capital — guess what it was."

Xiaoman couldn't guess.

"'Its tribute was earth of five colours' — five colours of earth. Green, red, white, black, yellow, each packed apart, carried a thousand li." He looked at Xiaoman. "That day in the main hall the testing stone lit up five colours and the whole hall laughed at you. They laughed that you were a dishrag patched from five colours of scraps."

Xiaoman lowered his head and said nothing.

"Four thousand years ago," said Elder Qu, "what King Yu wanted was exactly these five colours of earth."

Xiaoman's head came up with a jerk.

Elder Qu wasn't looking at him; he was looking at the Si far off. "The 'Tribute of Yu' has another line: 'Floating chime-stones from the banks of the Si' — the stones by the Si ring like a chime when struck." He picked up a flat bluestone at his feet and tapped it lightly with the broom handle.

*Donnng —*

Not loud, but long and far, like someone striking a bell very, very far away. Hearing it, something stirred in Xiaoman's heart — he seemed to have heard a sound like this somewhere, but couldn't remember where.

"Xun, the fourth, in the south-east, is Xu Province," said Elder Qu. "You're a Xu man. Today I'll teach you Xun Four first. The Si is where everything began."

He stood, turned the broom round in his hands, head down, handle forward. "Watch."

One movement only.

Xiaoman didn't even see how he moved; he only saw that the fallen leaves on the cliff top — none on the bluestone, but at the cliff edge beyond it a whole winter's leaves lay heaped — were swept up to the last one and hung in the air in a neat square grid, three to a row, nine squares, the middle one empty. Then the leaves came drifting down, one by one, onto the cliff top, and fell into a character:

**徐** — Xu

The character was missing its middle stroke.

Elder Qu leaned the broom back against the wall and dusted his hands. "Forty years' practice, and I've only got this far. That middle stroke — it's one element short. I can't fill it."

"Master, the canon is called Heluo. Luo is the Luo diagram — the nine palaces. Then what's He?"

"He is the River Chart." He crouched and with the broom handle drew a circle in the leaves, like snow, and set five dots on it. "The River Chart speaks of the five elements feeding each other: Wood feeds Fire, Fire feeds Earth, Earth feeds Metal, Metal feeds Water, Water feeds Wood again — one feeding the next, round in a circle. For sword qi to turn in the body it has to turn like that — each feeding the next, not one missing. Miss one, and the circle breaks, and at the break the sword qi leaks out." He rubbed out one of the dots. "What I lack is Fire. Forty years, and there's always a gap in the circle."

Looking at the circle with one dot missing, Xiaoman's heart suddenly ached. He thought of Master Chu in the lecture hall calling him a skimmer, and of Yinyue in the chamber of the hidden realm saying: you're not a skimmer any more, you're a water vat. So he wasn't the only one in the world who leaked.

For a while Xiaoman couldn't speak.

Elder Qu shouldered his broom and went toward the hut without looking back: "You have all five elements. Fill it in, then come and find me."

At the door he stopped again, back to Xiaoman: "That pill — before you take it, come and ask me first."

And he went in.

Xiaoman stood on the cliff top a while before starting down. Halfway down he looked back. The hut door was open; Elder Qu sat at the wooden table, not moving, the two cups before him, one up, one down. Too far to see what he was doing — only that he sat a long time, and never touched the cup that was turned down.
